e-9ca895cd06.text: READ THE LIMIT BEFORE USING THIS EDGE. No document located in this pass states any transfer of function, records, personnel or authority from SETKA-AN/SETKA-MO to SOYUZUFOTSENTR, and Project Condign - which describes both the Soviet state exploitation programme and SOYUZUFOTSENTR in the same chapter - does not name SETKA at all. What is documented is date adjacency and a shared principal: Condign dates SOYUZUFOTSENTR to 1990; the board dates the SETKA programmes 1978-1990/91; and the board already carries an edge vladimir-azhazha -> setka-program labelled 'ran the parallel public ufology centre after censorship lifted'. This edge makes that existing person-level assertion visible at institution level and nothing more. Reasoning, not evidence. If a later pass finds a document showing a formal succession, re-tier it; if a later pass finds the two were unconnected, delete it without loss.

e-ee250d54a1.text: This is the reason the node exists at all. SOYUZUFOTSENTR reaches this board not through Russian ufology literature but through a UK SECRET UK EYES ONLY Defence Intelligence Staff assessment, which places the centre inside a paragraph opening 'It[s] clear that the Former Soviet Union has taken the study of UAPs seriously and th[a]t this may well be related to a programme of understanding and exploiting certain UAP-related natural phenomena, such as plasmas.' The same chapter runs on to Popovich's 1990 All Union Ufology Association at the Air Force Academy, General of Aviation Igor Maltsev's 1990 release of pilot reports, Vsevolod Troitsky of the Russian Academy of Sciences chairing a Commission for the Study of Anomalous Propagation and Phenomena, and Sokolov's account of Soviet aircraft incidents. Condign treats the public centre and the state effort as one national picture. Verified line by line against the released OCR.

endpoints.label: SETKA-AN / SETKA-MO (later Galaktika, then Gorizont) - Soviet state anomalous phenomena programme
IZMIRAN - Pushkov Institute of Terrestrial Magnetism

e-f6f4380746.label: head institute of the Academy of Sciences branch
e-f6f4380746.text: Academician V. Migulin, director of IZMIRAN and a radio physicist specialising in oscillation theory, radio wave propagation and radiolocation, was made scientific head of the academic branch, and IZMIRAN was designated head institute. The four-to-five person working group there was headed by Yu. Platov, co-author of the programme's published account.

claimed.text: The same history says the programme was run from Moscow: the founding council of the Military-Industrial Commission met in the Kremlin in October 1977, and both the military executor and IZMIRAN were in the Moscow region.

According to Platov and Sokolov's history, the Academy's president asked the Military-Industrial Commission for an urgent research programme, the Commission's council noted that servicemen's reports sometimes involved disruption of military equipment, and two topics entered the 1978 defence plan: the military one on the phenomena's effect on equipment and personnel, the academic one on their physical nature.

The history says a General Staff directive of 1980 made the central military institute the collection centre and, for 13 years, put the army on watch for such phenomena across practically the whole USSR, every serviceman becoming without knowing it a potential participant; Stonehill and Mantle add that guidelines for the Soviet Navy were dated 7 March 1980.

Platov and Sokolov give three reasons for secrecy: the work formally sat in the classified defence plan, a military-technical origin was thought likely at first, and some properties, such as the absence of radar contrast and high manoeuvrability, might have military use; official papers used the term paranormal phenomenon instead of UFO.

Platov and Sokolov say the programme was among the cheapest defence works, paid from the executing organisations' own budgets with no special financing; Stonehill and Mantle add that it was renamed Galaktika in 1981 and Gorizont in 1986 and that a group analysed reports at the Academy until 1996.

Condign quotes a Sokolov describing 40 cases in which Soviet pilots encountered UFOs, were ordered to chase and then shoot, and lost control and crashed three times, twice fatally, after which pilots were told to observe and turn away.

One account of an Institute 22, created in 1978 by the Academy and the Ministry of Defence, says it investigated about 3,000 reports and left 5-10% unexplained; on the board's reading it is most likely the same apparatus as SETKA under another name.

Condign says Azhazha's institute reportedly developed filters and infrared and ultraviolet photography and obtained imagery of peculiar spheres and humanoid figures, adding that if the imagery exists it has never been published.

contested.text: Platov and Sokolov's history reports about 3,000 messages and over 400 events registered as extraordinary, more than 90% resolved as rocket launches or high-altitude balloons, and attributes Petrozavodsk itself to the launch of the Kosmos 955 satellite from Plesetsk.

The same history records no report of a landing, of contact with occupants, or of abduction in 13 years, and concludes that either the USSR was closed to alien visits or the extraterrestrial hypothesis fails.

The records point different ways: that history finds nothing anomalous, while critics quoted in another account allege the academic branch was a cover for a more serious military one, Condign judges the effort exploitation-driven, and the Sokolov quoted in Condign describes fatal pursuits.
The history itself leaves one series open: the 1984-87 flight emergencies at the Borisoglebsk air unit, with unknown objects on radar and seen by pilots, on which it says there is no consensus.

A 1977 preliminary report for the Academy concluded that the Petrozavodsk phenomenon could not be satisfactorily understood from the available data; northern European governments wrote asking whether it was Soviet weapons testing.

Condign names only Azhazha for the 1990 centre; the claim that the cosmonaut Pavel Popovich was its president rests on a secondary source, and the 1993 documents obtained by Knapp came from the Ministry of Defence via Colonel Boris Sokolov, not from the KGB file handed to Popovich. The board's link from the centre to SETKA is an inference with no document of transfer.
COMETA cites Soviet statistical studies as comparable to French ones, but on the board's reading this does not name SETKA or any Soviet body.

lead.text: According to the programme's own published history, co-written by Yury Platov and B. Sokolov, from 1978 to 1990 the Soviet Union ran a state programme on anomalous phenomena, SETKA, split between the Ministry of Defence and the Academy of Sciences, and it found nothing extraterrestrial; British defence intelligence judged that the Soviet effort may well have been related to a programme of exploiting such phenomena.

questions: Where are the Russian-language founding documents of SETKA, and do they match Platov and Sokolov's account?
Is the Sokolov quoted by Condign on fatal pursuits the same Sokolov who co-wrote a history finding no contact of any kind, and if so how are the two accounts reconciled?
Was the military branch more substantive than the academic one, as Stonehill and Mantle and Colonel Aleksandr Plaksin later argued?
Are Institute 22 and SETKA the same organisation?
What happened at Borisoglebsk between 1984 and 1987?
Did Azhazha's centre ever publish the imagery Condign says it reportedly obtained, and when did Azhazha die?

record.text: The UK's Project Condign, Volume 3, states that the Former Soviet Union clearly took the study of UAPs seriously and that this may well relate to a programme of understanding and exploiting UAP-related natural phenomena such as plasmas.
The same chapter summarises two Russian scientific papers in which 20-30 scientists appear to have researched the prevention of air target detection, followed by three redacted lines.

Condign records a UFO Commission created in 1989 under the USSR Union of Scientific and Engineering Societies and, in 1990, the inter-industry centre to coordinate records, with the rights of an Academy of Sciences institute, headed by V. G. Azhazha, a former naval submariner; its stated remit was ufology as a science of UFOs and their relation to the Earth's biotechnosphere.
IZMIRAN is the Pushkov Institute of Terrestrial Magnetism, Ionosphere and Radio Wave Propagation of the Russian Academy of Sciences, founded in 1939.

summary.text: Accounts of the programme trace it to a surge of reports in 1977-1978, especially the Petrozavodsk phenomenon of 20 September 1977, which Izvestia reported as an unidentified natural phenomenon: a huge star with beams of light that hung over the town like a jellyfish.

According to Platov and Sokolov, the programme had two branches: SETKA-MO, led from a central military research institute in the Moscow region, and SETKA-AN, whose head institute was IZMIRAN under Academician V. Migulin, with a small working group headed by Platov.

The main published account is the history co-written by Platov, who headed the academic working group, and B. Sokolov; the board carries its contents at Tier 2 and has obtained no Russian-language archival record of the founding documents.

As censorship lifted, a public Inter-Industry Ufology Research Centre with institute rights under the Academy of Sciences was set up in 1990, headed by Vladimir Azhazha; the board knows of it chiefly through a British intelligence report.
